scenarios.explanation: A data connection is not a power supply. Compare each device’s declared class reservation with its port’s source limit, then total the actual reservations. A 30 W-capable port does not always reserve 30 W: the supplied device class determines this model’s allocation. Several different compatible port arrangements can satisfy every device.
hints: A data-only port cannot supply PoE. Compare the device’s class reservation with the source type.
Check the total reserved source power; an unused enabled port reserves nothing in this model.
A class 4 AP needs a 30 W-capable source profile. Give every device a different compatible port.
scenarios.simplifications: Source check 2026-11-16local/17UTC: CCNA v1.1 objective 1.1.h and Cisco PoE guide. Bounded declared IEEE802.3af/at source/class reservations only; listed ports reserve in fixed order as an explicit teaching policy, not vendor admission/priority behavior. Source reservation is not delivered power or measured consumption. No physical detection, negotiation, LLDP/CDP, electrical faults, PoE++, external power, IOS CLI, data-plane connectivity or actual equipment. No host action runs.

scenarios.explanation: First distinguish the per-port source limit from the shared source budget. Moving a class 4 AP to a PoE+ port can expose a second problem: another device still reserves power. Preserve the phone, deliberately disconnect or disable the out-of-service display, and check that the AP and phone both receive allocations. Starving an optional device is not the same as retiring its attachment.
hints: A data-only port cannot supply PoE. Compare the device’s class reservation with the source type.
Check the total reserved source power; an unused enabled port reserves nothing in this model.
A port accepts one device. Disconnect its current device before reusing it; the out-of-service attachment must be deliberately retired.
